# Purpose and scope

This guideline documents the FLRef utilities for simulating fishery-dependent
and survey length-frequency distributions (LFDs) from an age-structured
`FLStock`, and how they connect to the `mse` package through the observation
error model `sampling.lfd.oem()`. Every step uses the North Sea plaice example
in FLCore (`data(ple4)`, `data(ple4.indices)`) so that each function can be run
and checked in isolation.

* **Part I** builds everything with one **annual** sampling step: one sample
  per gear and year, at a fixed time of the year.
* **Part II** moves the survey to **January** (a pulse survey) and samples the
  fishery **continuously** (quarterly or monthly), with a high length sample
  size and a moderate age (cluster) sample size, and contrasts the annual and
  continuous designs. The option `season` keeps the seasonal samples in the
  season dimension (`season = TRUE`, for a seasonal assessment) or pools them
  into an annual sample (`season = FALSE`, the default).
* **Part III** runs both designs inside an MSE with `sampling.lfd.oem()`.

The document is the first of a series:

| Doc | Stock structure | `unit` dimension | Status |
|-----|-----------------|------------------|--------|
| **1 (this)** | single sex, single area | `"unique"` | prototype |
| 2 | sex-structured (`data(ple4sex)`) | `c("F", "M")`, `unit.type = "gender"` | planned |
| 3 | spatial (areas as units) | area names, `unit.type = "spatial"` | planned, linked to the ICES deep-sea working group report |

The pipeline from the operating model (OM) to the estimator is:

```
FLStock (N, F, M)  ->  catch_n_gear()  ->  C[g,a,y]        (Baranov by gear)
                       season_fraction() -> C[g,a,y,s]    (within-year split, Part II)
                       survey_n_gear()   -> N e^{-Zt} s[a] (surveys)
lhpar  -> iALK()   ->  P(l|a,t)       ->  build_gear()    (s_g(l), P(l|a,g), design)
lfd.sim() / lfd.sim.season():  stage 1 age draw (ess_age), stage 2 length draw (ess_len)
sample_lfd_gears():  all of the above for a set of gears and years
sampling.lfd.oem():  sample_lfd_gears() for each data year inside mp()  ->  est
```

# Part I: annual sampling

## The example stock

```{r data}
data(ple4)
data(ple4.indices)

ages   <- an(dimnames(ple4)$age)
maxyr  <- dims(ple4)$maxyear
fbar_r <- unname(range(ple4)[c("minfbar", "maxfbar")])
pg     <- unname(range(ple4)["plusgroup"])

c(ages = range(ages), years = range(an(dimnames(ple4)$year)),
  fbar = fbar_r, plusgroup = pg)
names(ple4.indices)
summary(ple4.indices$IBTS_Q1)
```

`ple4` has a single `unit` (`"unique"`), one season and one area, and one
iteration. It provides the "true" numbers-at-age, F-at-age and weights; the
length dimension is added entirely through the growth model.

## Life history: a generic plaice growth curve

The length simulation needs a growth model, \(L(a) = L_\infty[1-e^{-k(a-t_0)}]\),
and, for raising samples to catch weight, a length-weight relationship
\(W = aL^b\). We take generic length-weight parameters for plaice and derive
\(L_\infty\), \(k\) and \(t_0\) so that they are consistent with the weights in
`ple4`: catch weights-at-age are converted to lengths by inverting \(W=aL^b\)
and a von Bertalanffy curve is fitted at mid-year (catch weights are
year-averages), excluding the plus group.

```{r lh-fit}
a_lw <- 8.9e-06   # generic plaice, W (kg) = a * L (cm)^b
b_lw <- 3.05

yrs_ref <- ac((maxyr - 9):maxyr)
w_a     <- c(yearMeans(catch.wt(ple4)[, yrs_ref]))
l_a     <- (w_a / a_lw)^(1 / b_lw)          # implied mean length in the catch
fit_age <- ages < pg                         # drop the plus group

vb_nll <- function(p) {
  pred <- p[1] * (1 - exp(-p[2] * (ages[fit_age] + 0.5 - p[3])))
  sum((log(l_a[fit_age]) - log(pmax(pred, 1e-3)))^2)
}
vb_fit <- optim(c(linf = 1.2 * max(l_a), k = 0.2, t0 = -0.5), vb_nll,
                method = "L-BFGS-B",
                lower = c(max(l_a), 0.05, -3), upper = c(2 * max(l_a), 1, 1))

lhpar <- FLPar(linf = vb_fit$par[["linf"]], k = vb_fit$par[["k"]],
               t0 = vb_fit$par[["t0"]], a = a_lw, b = b_lw)
lhpar
```

```{r lh-plot, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Mean length-at-age implied by ple4 catch weights (points) and the fitted von Bertalanffy curve at mid-year (line). The plus group (open point) is not used in the fit."}
vb_age <- seq(0, max(ages) + 1, 0.1)
ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(vb_age, c(lhpar["linf"]) *
                  (1 - exp(-c(lhpar["k"]) * (vb_age + 0.5 - c(lhpar["t0"]))))),
            colour = "#0b5d8a", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(ages, l_a, shape = fit_age), size = 2.2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 1), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Length (cm)") + theme_bw()
```

**Check.** With ages 1-9 only, \(L_\infty\) and \(k\) are partly confounded;
the fit only needs to reproduce lengths over the ages present in the stock.
If you have published growth parameters for the stock, use them directly in
`FLPar(linf =, k =, t0 =, a =, b =)` and check them with the plot above.

> **Sex-structured stocks (Doc 2).** `lhpar` will carry a second dimension,
> `unit = c("F", "M")`, so that `lhpar[, "F"]` lines up with `stk[, , "F"]`.
> See the last section.

## Inverse age-length key

`iALK()` builds \(P(l \mid a, t)\): normal length-at-age with
\(\mathrm{sd} = cv \cdot L(a+t)\), on the grid returned by `len_grid()`
(lower bin limits, last bin a plus group). Within-year time \(t\) enters as
\(t_0 - t\). Every downstream helper takes the grid from the gear
(`gear$grid`), so it is defined once here.

```{r ialk}
grid <- list(lmin = 5, lmax_mult = 1.2, bin = 1, cv = 0.1)
lens <- len_grid(c(lhpar["linf"]), grid$lmin, grid$lmax_mult, grid$bin)

ialk <- iALK(params = FLPar(linf = c(lhpar["linf"]), k = c(lhpar["k"]),
                            t0 = c(lhpar["t0"]) - 0.5),
             age = ages, cv = grid$cv, lmin = grid$lmin, bin = grid$bin,
             max = max(lens))
ialk_mat <- matrix(c(ialk), nrow = length(ages),
                   dimnames = list(age = ages, len = lens))
dim(ialk_mat)
```

```{r ialk-checks}
# rows are probability distributions
range(rowSums(ialk_mat))

# mean length by age reproduces the growth curve (up to grid truncation)
len_mid  <- lens + grid$bin / 2
mean_len <- c(ialk_mat %*% len_mid)
vb_len   <- c(lhpar["linf"]) * (1 - exp(-c(lhpar["k"]) * (ages + 0.5 - c(lhpar["t0"]))))
round(cbind(age = ages, iALK = mean_len, vonbert = vb_len), 1)
```

```{r ialk-plot, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Inverse age-length key P(l | a) at mid-year."}
df_ialk <- as.data.frame(as.table(ialk_mat), responseName = "p")
df_ialk$len <- an(as.character(df_ialk$len))
ggplot(df_ialk, aes(len, p, colour = age)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Length (cm)", y = "P(l | a)", colour = "Age") + theme_bw()
```

## Gears: one commercial fleet and one survey

Selectivity is specified **in length**, \(s_g(l)\), and integrated through the
inverse key to give selectivity-at-age and the capture-conditioned key:

\[
s_{g,a}=\sum_l P(l\mid a,t)\,s_g(l),\qquad
P(l\mid a,g)=\frac{P(l\mid a,t)\,s_g(l)}{s_{g,a}}.
\]

`build_gear()` returns both, the F partition, and the gear's **sampling
design**: `obs` (`"fishery"` or `"survey"`), `timing` and `n_seasons`. The
two gears are:

* **Commercial**: the fleet that takes all the catch (`f_mult = 1`), sampled
  at mid-year (`timing = 0.5`).
* **Survey**: the first-quarter International Bottom Trawl Survey
  (`ple4.indices$IBTS_Q1`). It removes no catch
  (`obs = "survey"` implies `f_mult = 0`), so the catch split by gear is
  `c(Commercial = 1, Survey = 0)`, but it has its own length selectivity,
  timing and sample size.

### Target selectivities-at-age from ple4

The length-selectivity parameters are chosen so that \(s_{g,a}\) reproduces
the age selectivities in the data: the mean exploitation pattern over the last
five years for the fleet, and the mean survey selectivity-at-age
(`sel.pattern(ple4.indices$IBTS_Q1)`) for the survey. Ages outside the survey
age range are left out of the survey fit.

```{r targets}
yrs_sel <- ac((maxyr - 4):maxyr)
sel_com <- yearMeans(harvest(ple4)[, yrs_sel])
sel_com <- c(sel_com / max(sel_com))

ibts  <- ple4.indices$IBTS_Q1
srv_t <- mean(range(ibts)[c("startf", "endf")])        # within-year timing (Q1)
if (!is.finite(srv_t)) srv_t <- 1 / 8

# survey selectivity-at-age as estimated in the assessment (sel.pattern)
sp      <- sel.pattern(ibts)
sp_mean <- apply(sp, c(1, 3:6), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
if (all(!is.finite(sp_mean))) {
  # fallback: empirical catchability-at-age, index / numbers at survey time
  yrs_i   <- intersect(dimnames(index(ibts))$year, dimnames(ple4)$year)
  n_i     <- (stock.n(ple4) * exp(-(harvest(ple4) + m(ple4)) * srv_t))[
               dimnames(index(ibts))$age, yrs_i]
  sp_mean <- apply(index(ibts)[, yrs_i] / n_i, c(1, 3:6), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
}
ages_i  <- intersect(dimnames(sp_mean)$age, ac(ages))  # survey ages in the stock
sp_i    <- c(sp_mean[ages_i])
sel_srv <- setNames(rep(NA_real_, length(ages)), ages)
sel_srv[ages_i] <- sp_i / max(sp_i, na.rm = TRUE)

round(rbind(Commercial = sel_com, Survey = sel_srv), 2)
c(survey_timing = srv_t)
```

### Fitting length selectivity to the age targets

The helper below is written for this guideline; it may become an FLRef
function (`fit_gear_sel()`). It minimises the squared difference between
the ALK-integrated \(s_{g,a}\) from `build_gear()` and the target, so the fitted
length curve is exactly the one the gear object will use.

An unconstrained fit is not enough. Age targets can be matched by
unrealistic length curves: a dome in age, for instance, is reproduced
almost as well by a near-vertical "cliff" in length, and a survey that
catches mostly age 1 by a curve that only declines from the smallest length
class. A length selectivity should always have an **ascending limb** and a
**gradually curved descending limb**. The double-normal is therefore fitted
in a parameterisation that guarantees both:

\[
\sigma_L = e^{q_2},\qquad
L_{peak} = l_{min} + 2.5\,\sigma_L + e^{q_1},\qquad
\sigma_R = \sigma_L\,(1 + e^{q_3}).
\]

* \(L_{peak} \ge l_{min} + 2.5\sigma_L\) means selectivity in the smallest
  length class is at most \(e^{-2.5^2/2} \approx 0.04\): the ascending limb
  is always inside the length grid.
* \(\sigma_R \ge \sigma_L\) means the descending limb is never steeper than
  the ascending one, so it is a curved dome and not a cliff; large
  \(\sigma_R\) approaches asymptotic (logistic-like) selectivity.
* Bounds keep \(\sigma_L\) between `sd_min` and \(0.3L_\infty\), and
  \(L_{peak}\) below \(L_\infty\).

```{r fit-sel}
fit_gear_sel <- function(target, lhpar, age, type = c("dnormal", "logistic"),
                         timing = 0.5, grid, sd_min = 1) {
  type <- match.arg(type)
  ok   <- is.finite(target)
  linf <- c(lhpar["linf"])
  l_at <- linf * (1 - exp(-c(lhpar["k"]) * (age + timing - c(lhpar["t0"]))))

  mk <- function(q) switch(type,
    logistic = list(type = "logistic", L50 = grid$lmin + exp(q[1]),
                    L95 = grid$lmin + exp(q[1]) + exp(q[2])),
    dnormal  = {
      sdl <- exp(q[2])
      list(type = "dnormal", Lpeak = grid$lmin + 2.5 * sdl + exp(q[1]),
           sd_left = sdl, sd_right = sdl * (1 + exp(q[3])))
    })

  sel_a <- function(q) {
    cfg <- c(mk(q), f_mult = 1, ess_age = 1, ess_len = 1)
    g <- build_gear(list(G = cfg), lhpar = lhpar, age = age, timing = timing,
                    lmin = grid$lmin, lmax_mult = grid$lmax_mult,
                    bin = grid$bin, cv = grid$cv)$G
    c(g$sel_a)
  }
  obj <- function(q) sum((sel_a(q)[ok] - target[ok])^2)

  # start: peak at the length of the age with maximum target selectivity
  l_pk <- l_at[ok][which.max(target[ok])]
  if (type == "dnormal") {
    sdl0  <- max(sd_min, 0.15 * l_pk)
    q0    <- c(log(max(l_pk - grid$lmin - 2.5 * sdl0, 1)), log(sdl0), 0)
    lower <- c(log(0.5), log(sd_min), log(0.05))
    upper <- c(log(linf), log(0.3 * linf), log(20))
  } else {
    l50   <- approx(target[ok], l_at[ok], 0.5, ties = mean)$y
    q0    <- c(log(max(l50 - grid$lmin, 1)), log(5))
    lower <- c(log(0.5), log(0.5))
    upper <- c(log(linf), log(0.5 * linf))
  }
  q0  <- pmin(pmax(q0, lower), upper)
  opt <- optim(q0, obj, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = lower, upper = upper)
  list(cfg = mk(opt$par), sel_a = sel_a(opt$par), ssq = opt$value,
       at_bound = any(abs(opt$par - lower) < 1e-6 | abs(opt$par - upper) < 1e-6))
}

fit_com <- fit_gear_sel(sel_com, lhpar, ages, "dnormal", timing = 0.5, grid = grid)
fit_srv <- fit_gear_sel(sel_srv, lhpar, ages, "dnormal", timing = srv_t, grid = grid)

fit_tab <- function(...) {
  fits <- list(...)
  t(sapply(fits, function(f) c(unlist(f$cfg[-1]), ssq = f$ssq,
                               at_bound = f$at_bound)))
}
round(fit_tab(Commercial = fit_com, Survey = fit_srv), 3)
```

**Check.** `at_bound = 1` means a parameter sits on a bound: the age target
asks for a shape the constraints do not allow (typically a very steep dome).
That is acceptable when the plots below look reasonable, because the
constraint is deliberate; the fitted selectivity-at-age will then only
"roughly" match the target at the oldest ages.

### Building the gear objects

Both gears are built in one call. The survey's own `timing` overrides the
call-level default (mid-year), so its capture-conditioned key is evaluated at
the time of the survey. Because the survey has `f_mult = 0`, its F share is
zero and the commercial share is one at every age.

```{r build-gear}
build_design <- function(cfg)
  build_gear(cfg, lhpar = lhpar, age = ages, timing = 0.5,
             lmin = grid$lmin, lmax_mult = grid$lmax_mult,
             bin = grid$bin, cv = grid$cv, fbar_range = fbar_r)

om_gears <- build_design(list(
  Commercial = c(fit_com$cfg, f_mult = 1, ess_age = 50, ess_len = 300),
  Survey     = c(fit_srv$cfg, obs = "survey", ess_age = 30, ess_len = 200,
                 timing = srv_t)))

data.frame(obs = gear_par(om_gears, "obs"), f_mult = gear_par(om_gears, "f_mult"),
           timing = sapply(om_gears, function(g) g$grid$timing),
           n_seasons = gear_par(om_gears, "n_seasons"),
           ess_age = gear_par(om_gears, "ess_age"),
           ess_len = gear_par(om_gears, "ess_len"))
```

```{r gear-checks}
# capture-conditioned keys: rows sum to one; all components share one grid
sapply(om_gears, function(gr) c(
  rowsum_min = min(rowSums(gr$condALK)), rowsum_max = max(rowSums(gr$condALK)),
  length_bins = ncol(gr$condALK),
  same_grid = identical(colnames(gr$condALK), dimnames(gr$sel_len)$len)))

# static F shares: the catch split is c(1, 0) at every age
round(rbind(Commercial = c(om_gears$Commercial$f_share),
            Survey     = c(om_gears$Survey$f_share)), 3)

# joint selectivity equals the commercial selectivity for a single fishing gear
round(rbind(joint = c(joint_sel(om_gears)),
            commercial = c(om_gears$Commercial$sel_a) /
              max(om_gears$Commercial$sel_a)), 3)
```

```{r gear-plot-len, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Fitted selectivity-at-length."}
df_l <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(om_gears), function(g)
  data.frame(gear = g, len = om_gears[[g]]$len_bins$mid,
             sel = c(om_gears[[g]]$sel_len))))
ggplot(df_l, aes(len, sel, colour = gear)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "Length (cm)", y = "s(l)", colour = NULL) + theme_bw()
```

```{r gear-plot-age, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "ALK-integrated selectivity-at-age from build_gear() (lines) against the ple4 targets (points)."}
df_a <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(om_gears), function(g)
  data.frame(gear = g, age = ages, sel = c(om_gears[[g]]$sel_a),
             target = if (g == "Commercial") sel_com else sel_srv)))
ggplot(df_a, aes(age, sel, colour = gear)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(y = target)) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "s(a)", colour = NULL) + theme_bw()
```

```{r condalk-plot, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Capture-conditioned key P(l | a, g) for the commercial gear, with mean length-at-age in the population (solid) and in the catch (dashed): young ages are caught at above-average length."}
plot_condALK(om_gears$Commercial, params = TRUE)
```

## Partitioning the true catch by gear

`catch_n_gear()` is the single definition of gear catch used by the OM and by
`sampling.lfd.oem()`:

\[
C_{g,a,y}=N_{a,y}\,\frac{\phi_{g,a}F_{a,y}}{Z_{a,y}}\left(1-e^{-Z_{a,y}}\right),
\qquad \sum_g \phi_{g,a}=1 .
\]

```{r catch-gear}
yrs <- ac((maxyr - 9):maxyr)            # the "data years" used below
cn  <- catch_n_gear(ple4, om_gears, years = yrs)

# catch split by gear, as passed to e.g. FLicc (catch_by_gear)
catch_by_gear(cn, ple4, years = yrs)

# Baranov total vs. catch.n in ple4 (assessment-consistent but not identical)
rel <- attr(cn, "total") / catch.n(ple4)[, yrs]
round(range(rel, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
```

The survey "catch" is not a removal. What the survey samples is numbers at the
time of the survey, weighted by survey selectivity-at-age,
\(I_{a,y}=N_{a,y}e^{-Z_{a,y}t_s}s_{\mathrm{srv},a}\) (`survey_n_gear()`).

```{r survey-n}
in_srv <- survey_n_gear(ple4, om_gears$Survey, years = yrs)
```

## Single-stage length sampling: `len.sim()`

`len.sim()` projects an at-age composition through the key and draws one
multinomial length sample of size `ess`. Without a gear it uses the biological
key \(P(l\mid a)\); with a gear it uses \(P(l\mid a,g)\). The difference matters:
within an age class the gear selects by length.

```{r len-sim}
set.seed(1)
lfd_bio  <- len.sim(cn$Commercial, params = lhpar, ess = 300, timing = 0.5,
                    bin = grid$bin, cv = grid$cv, lmin = grid$lmin,
                    lmax = grid$lmax_mult)
lfd_gear <- len.sim(cn$Commercial, params = lhpar, ess = 300, timing = 0.5,
                    gear = om_gears$Commercial)

mean_len_lfd <- function(x) c(quantSums(x * an(dimnames(x)$len)) / quantSums(x))
round(rbind(biological_key = mean_len_lfd(lfd_bio),
            gear_key       = mean_len_lfd(lfd_gear)), 1)
```

## Two-stage sampling: `lfd.sim()`

### Rationale

Fish in a length sample are not independent draws from the catch. They are
collected in clusters (hauls, trips, boxes landed at a market), and fish
within a cluster are more alike in size and age than fish from different
clusters, because each haul or trip fishes a particular place, depth and time
where some cohorts dominate. The information in a length composition is
therefore governed by the number of clusters more than by the number of fish
measured, and the effective sample size (ESS) of a length composition is
usually a small fraction of the number of fish measured. A single-stage
multinomial with the nominal number of fish makes simulated data far too
precise, so an assessment fitted to them shows unrealistically narrow
uncertainty, and an MSE built on them is over-optimistic about length-based
advice.

`lfd.sim()` generates the clustering from the population structure itself,
with a hierarchical two-stage design:

1. **Stage 1 (clusters to ages).** A multinomial **age** sample of size
   \(n_A\) = `ess_age` from the true catch-at-age composition (via
   `ca.sim()`),
   \[
   \mathbf{x}\sim\mathrm{Mult}(n_A,\mathbf{p}),\qquad
   p_a=\frac{C_{g,a}}{\sum_{a'}C_{g,a'}},\qquad \hat p_a=\frac{x_a}{n_A}.
   \]
   \(n_A\) is the number of effectively independent age draws: roughly the
   number of sampled clusters times the effective number of distinct fish
   per cluster.
2. **Stage 2 (fish to lengths).** A multinomial **length** sample of size
   \(n_L\) = `ess_len` from the sampled age composition projected through the
   capture-conditioned key \(K_{a,l}=P(l\mid a,g)\),
   \[
   \mathbf{y}\sim\mathrm{Mult}(n_L,\hat{\boldsymbol\pi}),\qquad
   \hat\pi_l=\sum_a\hat p_a K_{a,l},\qquad o_l=\frac{y_l}{n_L}.
   \]

The sample is unbiased, \(E[o_l]=\pi_l=\sum_a p_aK_{a,l}\), and its variance
follows from the law of total variance:

\[
\mathrm{Var}(o_l)=\frac{\pi_l(1-\pi_l)}{n_L}
+\left(1-\frac{1}{n_L}\right)V_l,\qquad
V_l=\mathrm{Var}(\hat\pi_l)=\frac{1}{n_A}\left(\sum_a p_aK_{a,l}^2-\pi_l^2\right).
\]

The first term is the ordinary multinomial noise of measuring \(n_L\) fish;
the second is the extra (between-cluster) noise from the age stage. Summing
over length bins gives the expected effective sample size,

\[
ESS=\frac{\sum_l\pi_l(1-\pi_l)}{\sum_l\mathrm{Var}(o_l)} .
\]

Three limits help to choose the sample sizes:

* \(n_A\to\infty\): \(ESS\to n_L\), the single-stage multinomial.
* \(n_L\to\infty\): \(ESS\to\sum_l\pi_l(1-\pi_l)/\sum_lV_l\ge n_A\). A
  length bin mixes several ages, which averages out part of the age-stage
  noise, so the length composition is somewhat more informative than the age
  sample it came from.
* Ages that do not overlap in length: \(ESS\approx(1/n_A+1/n_L)^{-1}\).

In practice `ess_age` is small (tens: the number of hauls or trips) and
`ess_len` large (hundreds to thousands of fish), and the realised ESS lies
between \(n_A\) and \(n_L\), closer to \(n_A\) when \(n_L\gg n_A\). Unlike an
overdispersion parameter (e.g. a Dirichlet-multinomial), the age stage makes
the ESS respond to the stock and the gear: a catch dominated by one strong
year class or a gear with narrow selectivity gives a different ESS for the
same `ess_age`, as real sampling programmes do.

**Within-year sampling (Part II).** Each season is an independent two-stage
sample with \(n_{A,s}\) and \(n_{L,s}\) summing to the annual totals. For the
pooled annual composition the seasonal variances add with weights
\((n_{L,s}/n_L)^2\), so splitting the same totals among seasons leaves the
annual ESS roughly unchanged. What continuous sampling changes is the
**target**, the year-round catch composition instead of a snapshot (Part II).

```{r lfd-sim}
lfd_com <- lfd.sim(cn$Commercial, om_gears$Commercial)        # scaled to catch numbers
lfd_srv <- lfd.sim(in_srv,        om_gears$Survey)
```

`sample_lfd_gears()` does the same for a whole gear list in one call, with
exactly the code that `sampling.lfd.oem()` runs inside the MSE (raw counts,
not scaled):

```{r sample-gears}
smp_a <- sample_lfd_gears(ple4, om_gears, years = yrs)
sapply(smp_a$lfd, function(x) range(c(quantSums(x))))   # = ess_len per year
```

```{r ridge, fig.height = 7, fig.cap = "Simulated commercial and survey length samples with von Bertalanffy cohort lines."}
plot_lfd_ridgeline(list(Commercial = lfd_com, Survey = lfd_srv), lhpar = lhpar)
```

### Check: realised effective sample size

For a multinomial sample the McAllister-Ianelli estimator
\(\widehat{ESS}=\sum_l p_l(1-p_l)\big/\sum_l(o_l-p_l)^2\) recovers the sample
size. Replicating one year many times shows that the single-stage sampler
returns `ess`, while the two-stage sampler returns an effective sample size
well below `ess_len`, which is the intended behaviour.

```{r ess-check}
nrep <- 500
x    <- propagate(cn$Commercial[, ac(maxyr)], nrep)
gC   <- om_gears$Commercial
p_true <- c((c(cn$Commercial[, ac(maxyr)]) / sum(cn$Commercial[, ac(maxyr)])) %*%
              gC$condALK)

ess_mi <- function(lfd, p) {
  if (dim(lfd)[4] > 1) lfd <- seasonSums(lfd)
  o <- matrix(c(lfd), ncol = dims(lfd)$iter)
  o <- sweep(o, 2, colSums(o), "/")
  sum(p * (1 - p)) / colSums((o - p)^2)
}
one <- len.sim(x, params = lhpar, ess = gC$ess_len, timing = 0.5,
               gear = gC, scale = FALSE)
two <- lfd.sim(x, gC, scale = FALSE)

c(ess_len = gC$ess_len, ess_age = gC$ess_age,
  single_stage = median(ess_mi(one, p_true)),
  two_stage    = median(ess_mi(two, p_true)))
```

### Check: theory against simulation

The variance formula gives the expected ESS without simulation. It is
compared here with the simulated ESS (as a ratio of means,
\(\sum_l\pi_l(1-\pi_l)/\overline{\sum_l(o_l-\pi_l)^2}\), which is the quantity
the formula predicts) over a range of `ess_age` for `ess_len = 300`.

```{r ess-theory}
ess_two_stage <- function(p_a, K, n_A, n_L) {
  p_a <- p_a / sum(p_a)
  pl  <- c(p_a %*% K)
  V   <- (c(p_a %*% K^2) - pl^2) / n_A
  sum(pl * (1 - pl)) / sum(pl * (1 - pl) / n_L + (1 - 1 / n_L) * V)
}
ess_rm <- function(lfd, p) {
  o <- matrix(c(lfd), ncol = dims(lfd)$iter)
  o <- sweep(o, 2, colSums(o), "/")
  sum(p * (1 - p)) / mean(colSums((o - p)^2))
}

p_a0  <- c(cn$Commercial[, ac(maxyr)])
n_Ag  <- c(10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 1000)
ess_g <- t(sapply(n_Ag, function(nA) {
  sim <- lfd.sim(propagate(cn$Commercial[, ac(maxyr)], 300), gC,
                 ess_age = nA, ess_len = 300, scale = FALSE)
  c(ess_age = nA, predicted = ess_two_stage(p_a0, gC$condALK, nA, 300),
    simulated = ess_rm(sim, p_true))
}))
round(ess_g)
```

```{r ess-theory-plot, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Expected (line) and simulated (points) effective sample size of a two-stage length sample with ess_len = 300 (dotted) as a function of ess_age; the dashed line is the 1:1 line ESS = ess_age."}
ggplot(as.data.frame(ess_g), aes(ess_age)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predicted), colour = "#0b5d8a", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(y = simulated), size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 300, linetype = 3) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "ess_age (log scale)", y = "Effective sample size (log scale)") +
  theme_bw()
```

### Why the ESS lies above `ess_age`: the growth curve

The age stage adds \(V_l=\mathrm{Var}_{a\sim p}(K_{a,l})/n_A\), the variance
across ages of the probability that a fish of age \(a\) falls in length class
\(l\). It is large only when ages put their fish in different length classes.
If every length class belonged to a single age, an extra fish of age 3 in the
age sample would show up one-to-one in the length composition and
\(ESS\approx(1/n_A+1/n_L)^{-1}\), on the 1:1 line. If all ages had the same
length distribution, age-sampling errors would be invisible in length
(\(V_l=0\)) and \(ESS=n_L\).

The von Bertalanffy curve decides where a stock lies between these extremes.
The spacing between consecutive ages shrinks geometrically,
\(\bar L_{a+1}-\bar L_a=(L_\infty-\bar L_a)(1-e^{-k})\), while the spread
within an age grows, \(\sigma_a=cv\,\bar L_a\). The separation of neighbouring
ages, \(d_a=(\bar L_{a+1}-\bar L_a)/\sigma_a\), is therefore large for young
fish on the steep part of the curve and falls towards zero as
\(\bar L_a\to L_\infty\). Age-sampling noise among young, well-separated ages
passes through to the length composition. Among old ages piled up near
\(L_\infty\) it largely cancels: too many age-8 and too few age-9 fish hardly
change the length composition. The more of the catch lies on the flat part
of the curve (slow growth, small \(k\), large CV, a gear that cuts out the
young ages), the further the ESS rises above `ess_age`. The flip side is the
backward check below: where ages overlap in length, the length composition
cannot tell them apart, so ALK errors are largest at the oldest ages.

```{r age-separation}
K   <- gC$condALK
ovl <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(K) - 1), function(i) sum(pmin(K[i, ], K[i + 1, ])))
sep <- data.frame(
  ages        = paste(ages[-length(ages)], ages[-1], sep = "-"),
  mean_length = round(mean_len[-length(ages)], 1),
  spacing     = round(diff(mean_len), 1),                     # cm between ages
  d           = round(diff(mean_len) / (grid$cv * mean_len[-length(ages)]), 2),
  overlap     = round(ovl, 2),                                # shared length mass
  catch_share = round(p_a0[-length(ages)] / sum(p_a0), 2))
sep
```

`d` is the separation of neighbouring ages in standard deviations of length,
`overlap` the probability mass the two capture-conditioned length
distributions share (0 = separate, 1 = identical), and `catch_share` the
share of the younger age in the catch. Ages with a large catch share and high
overlap are the ones that lift the ESS above `ess_age`.

### Check: common random numbers

Inside an MSE each management procedure must see the same sampling noise.
`rUnif_lfd()` pre-generates the uniforms for both stages and `rmultinom_crn()`
turns them into multinomial draws. Same deviates give the same sample; a small
change in the catch moves only a few fish between neighbouring bins.

```{r crn}
u <- rUnif_lfd(om_gears, years = yrs, nsim = 1, seed = 456)
s1 <- lfd.sim(cn$Commercial, gC, u_age = u$age$Commercial, u_len = u$len$Commercial,
              scale = FALSE)
s2 <- lfd.sim(cn$Commercial, gC, u_age = u$age$Commercial, u_len = u$len$Commercial,
              scale = FALSE)
identical(s1, s2)

cn_pert <- cn$Commercial
cn_pert[1, ] <- cn_pert[1, ] * 1.05          # 5% more age-1 fish
s3 <- lfd.sim(cn_pert, gC, u_age = u$age$Commercial, u_len = u$len$Commercial,
              scale = FALSE)
c(fish_moved_per_year = mean(c(quantSums(abs(s3 - s1)))) / 2,
  sample_size = gC$ess_len)
```

## Backward check: from length samples back to catch-at-age

A forward simulator should pass a backward test: if an assessment converts the
simulated length samples back to ages with an age-length key (ALK), it should
recover the OM catch-at-age (`catch.n`), apart from sampling error. This also
shows which part of the error comes from the length sample and which from the
ALK.

For gear \(g\), year \(y\) and length class \(l\), the ALK is the
distribution of age given length in the catch,

\[
P(a\mid l,g)=\frac{C_{g,a}\,P(l\mid a,g)}{\sum_{a'}C_{g,a'}\,P(l\mid a',g)},
\]

and the catch-at-age estimate from a length sample \(n_l\) is
\(\hat n_a=\sum_l n_l\,P(a\mid l,g)\), raised to the gear's catch weight by
sum of products, \(\tilde n_a=\hat n_a\,C^{w}_{g}\big/\sum_{a'}\hat n_{a'}w_{a'}\).
Two estimates are compared with the true gear catch-at-age \(C_{g,a,y}\)
(`catch_n_gear()`), all raised in the same way:

| Estimate | Data | Errors included |
|---|---|---|
| **True ALK** | two-stage LFD \(\times\) exact \(P(a\mid l,g)\) | length sampling |
| **Sampled ALK** | two-stage LFD \(\times\) ALK from a length-stratified otolith subsample (`alk.sample()`, at most `nbin` fish per length class) | length sampling + ALK sampling: the realistic case |

The key must be the capture-conditioned one: the gear selects by length
within an age class, so young ages are caught at above-average length (see
the capture-conditioned key above), and a key built from the biological
\(P(l\mid a)\) would assign these fish to older ages.

```{r back-setup}
as_flpar <- function(m) FLPar(array(m, dim = c(dim(m), 1)),
                              dimnames = list(age = rownames(m), len = colnames(m),
                                              iter = 1))
raise_sop <- function(x, cw, wt) x %*% (cw / quantSums(x * wt))
col_bc <- c(True = "black", `True ALK` = "#0072B2", `Sampled ALK` = "#CC3311")

cn_true  <- cn$Commercial                              # true gear catch-at-age
cw_true  <- catch_gear(cn, ple4)$Commercial            # true gear catch weight
wt_c     <- catch.wt(ple4)[, yrs]
alk_true <- ALKs(cn_true, as_flpar(gC$condALK))         # P(a | l, g), by year

back_calc <- function(seed, nbin = 20) {
  set.seed(seed)
  lfd <- lfd.sim(cn_true, gC, scale = FALSE)            # two-stage length sample
  alk_obs <- alk.sample(lfd, alk_true, nbin = nbin)     # otolith subsample
  est <- list(
    `True ALK`          = applyALK(lfd, alk_true),
    `Sampled ALK`       = applyALK(lfd, alk_obs))
  out <- FLQuants(lapply(est, function(x) {
    x <- FLQuant(c(x), dimnames = dimnames(cn_true))   # common dimnames
    raise_sop(x, cw_true, wt_c)
  }))
  attr(out, "otoliths") <- sum(sapply(alk_obs, sum))
  out
}

bc1 <- back_calc(1)
c(otoliths_per_year = attr(bc1, "otoliths") / length(yrs),
  fish_measured_per_year = gC$ess_len)
```

```{r back-years, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 9, fig.cap = "Backward check for one replicate: catch-at-age reconstructed from the simulated commercial length samples, by year, against the true gear catch-at-age (black)."}
df_bc <- as.data.frame(FLQuants(c(list(True = cn_true), as.list(bc1))))
df_bc$qname <- factor(df_bc$qname, levels = c("True", names(bc1)))
ggplot(df_bc, aes(age, data, colour = qname, linewidth = qname == "True")) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1.1, `FALSE` = 0.6), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col_bc) +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol = 5, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Catch numbers (thousands)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r back-ts, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 9, fig.cap = "Backward check for one replicate: time series by age."}
ggplot(df_bc, aes(year, data, colour = qname)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col_bc) +
  facet_wrap(~age, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Catch numbers (thousands)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Replicating the whole sampling chain separates bias (a shifted median) from
noise (a wide interval):

```{r back-reps}
nrep_bc <- 50
bc <- lapply(seq_len(nrep_bc), back_calc)

rel_err <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(bc), function(r)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(bc[[r]]), function(m) {
    d <- as.data.frame((bc[[r]][[m]] - cn_true) / cn_true)
    data.frame(rep = r, method = m, age = d$age, year = d$year, rel = d$data)
  }))))
rel_err$method <- factor(rel_err$method, levels = names(bc1))

# median relative error (bias) and median absolute relative error (precision)
tab_bc <- aggregate(rel ~ method + age, rel_err, function(x)
  c(bias = median(x), mare = median(abs(x))))
tab_bc <- do.call(data.frame, tab_bc)
round(xtabs(rel.bias ~ method + age, tab_bc), 2)
round(xtabs(rel.mare ~ method + age, tab_bc), 2)
```

```{r back-reps-plot, fig.height = 4.2, fig.width = 9, fig.cap = "Relative error of the reconstructed catch-at-age over 50 replicates and 10 years: median (point) and 5-95% range (bar). A median away from zero is bias; the bar width is sampling noise."}
q_bc <- aggregate(rel ~ method + age, rel_err, quantile, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
q_bc <- do.call(data.frame, q_bc)
names(q_bc)[3:5] <- c("lo", "med", "hi")
ggplot(q_bc, aes(factor(age), med, colour = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), position = position_dodge(0.6),
                  size = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col_bc[-1]) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1, 1.5)) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Relative error", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

What to look for:

* **True ALK** should be unbiased at all ages; its noise is the length-sample
  noise, i.e. the two-stage ESS, propagated to ages.
* **Sampled ALK** adds noise mainly at the oldest ages, where few large fish
  are available for otoliths, and some bias where length classes receive one
  or no otoliths (those fish are dropped before raising).

`ALKs()` is used with one iteration here; for several iterations see the
developer notes.

## Raising length samples to catch weight

`lfd_sop()` is the length analogue of `sops()`: it scales each sample so that
its sum of products with weight-at-length, \(W(l)=a\bar l^{\,b}\), equals the
catch weight.

```{r sop}
cw         <- catch_gear(cn, ple4)$Commercial
lfd_raised <- lfd_sop(lfd_com, gC, cw)

w <- lfd_raised
w[] <- gC$wt_len[dimnames(lfd_raised)$len]
# by construction, the raised SOP equals the catch weight
round(c(quantSums(lfd_raised * w) / cw), 6)
# diagnostic: raised numbers / true catch numbers. Departures from one
#     measure the mismatch between W(l), the growth curve and catch.wt
round(c(quantSums(lfd_raised) / quantSums(cn$Commercial)), 3)
```

# Part II: within-year sampling, pulse survey and continuous fishery sampling

## Why the sampling time matters

Part I measured all commercial fish at one moment, mid-year. Fishery sampling
programmes do not work like that: market and on-board samples are taken
throughout the year, and the annual length composition is the pool of many
small samples. Two things change within the year and are lost in a single
mid-year sample:

1. **Growth.** Each cohort grows during the year, so a cohort sampled in
   January is shorter than the same cohort in December. Pooling samples over
   the year smears each cohort mode over its within-year growth increment.
2. **Depletion.** Under constant F and M, more of the annual catch is taken
   early in the year, when numbers are highest, and the age composition of
   the catch shifts towards younger fish as older cohorts are fished down.

A survey, in contrast, is a **pulse**: all fish are measured within a few
weeks. Placed in January, it samples every cohort at nearly the same point of
its growth curve, before the growing season, so the cohort modes of young
ages are sharp. Combining a pulse survey with continuous fishery sampling is a
common data situation, and a seasonal assessment (e.g. FLicc with seasonal
transitions) can only exploit it if the samples keep their timing.

The annual OM in FLRef does not need seasons for this. The observation model
splits the annual gear catch-at-age into \(S\) equal seasons (next section)
and draws an independent two-stage sample in each season, with the
conditional key at the season mid-point \((s-0.5)/S\). The annual `ess_age`
and `ess_len` are split among seasons, so
a monthly design with `ess_age = 200`, `ess_len = 1000` measures about 83
fish a month from about 17 independent clusters: high length sample size, moderate
age (cluster) sample size.

## How the annual stock is seasonalised

The operating model stays annual: `stock.n`, `harvest` and `m` are annual and
the annual catch is the Baranov catch. Seasons exist only on the observation
side, which is why any annual `FLom` can be sampled monthly.

### Within-year dynamics

Within year \(y\), let \(t\in[0,1)\) be the time since 1 January, with ages
incremented on 1 January (the "birthday") and recruitment entering at
\(t=0\). With constant instantaneous rates \(F_{a}\) and \(M_{a}\) during the
year, \(Z_a=F_a+M_a\) (year index dropped),

\[
N_a(t)=N_a(0)\,e^{-Z_a t},\qquad
\frac{dC_{g,a}}{dt}=F_{g,a}\,N_a(t),\qquad F_{g,a}=\phi_{g,a}F_a .
\]

The catch of gear \(g\) between \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) is

\[
C_{g,a}(t_1,t_2)=\frac{F_{g,a}}{Z_a}\,N_a(0)\left(e^{-Z_at_1}-e^{-Z_at_2}\right),
\]

which for \((t_1,t_2)=(0,1)\) is the annual Baranov catch of `catch_n_gear()`.
For \(S\) equal seasons, season \(s\) is \([(s-1)/S,\,s/S)\) and

\[
C_{g,a,s}=C_{g,a}\,\pi_{a,s},\qquad
\pi_{a,s}=\frac{e^{-Z_a(s-1)/S}\left(1-e^{-Z_a/S}\right)}{1-e^{-Z_a}},
\qquad \sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_{a,s}=1
\]

(\(\pi_{a,s}=1/S\) when \(Z_a=0\)). This is `season_fraction()`. Because
the gear shares \(\phi_{g,a}\) are constant within the year, \(\pi\) is the
same for every gear, and the seasonal catches sum exactly to the annual
catch. Older, heavily fished ages (high \(Z\)) have their catch concentrated
early in the year.

### Within-year growth and the seasonal key

Fish caught in season \(s\) are assigned the length distribution at the
season mid-point \(t_s=(s-0.5)/S\):

\[
\bar L_a(t_s)=L_\infty\left(1-e^{-k(a+t_s-t_0)}\right),\qquad
P(l\mid a,t_s)=\text{iALK with } t_0\to t_0-t_s,
\]

and conditioned on the (time-invariant) length selectivity of the gear,
\(K_{a,l}(t_s)=P(l\mid a,t_s)s_g(l)\big/\sum_{l'}P(l'\mid a,t_s)s_g(l')\). The
expected length composition of the season-\(s\) catch and of the year-round
catch are

\[
\pi_{l,s}=\frac{\sum_aC_{g,a,s}K_{a,l}(t_s)}{\sum_aC_{g,a,s}},\qquad
\pi_l^{\text{year}}=\frac{\sum_s\sum_aC_{g,a,s}K_{a,l}(t_s)}{\sum_aC_{g,a}}
\;\xrightarrow{S\to\infty}\;
\frac{\int_0^1\sum_a\frac{dC_{g,a}}{dt}K_{a,l}(t)\,dt}{\sum_aC_{g,a}} .
\]

A single annual sample at \(t=0.5\) targets \(\sum_aC_{g,a}K_{a,l}(0.5)\)
instead, which differs from \(\pi_l^{\text{year}}\) through both growth (\(K\)
changes with \(t\)) and depletion (\(C\) is front-loaded).

### Assumptions and their limits

* Constant F and M within the year: no seasonal fishing pattern. A seasonal
  effort profile would replace \(F_a\) by \(F_ae_s\) with \(\sum_se_s/S=1\);
  this is not implemented yet.
* Growth is evaluated at the season mid-point; within-season growth is
  ignored (about one month of growth for monthly sampling).
* Birthday and recruitment on 1 January, consistent with the annual OM.
* The plus group is treated like any other age (its length distribution is
  that of the plus-group age).

### FLRef functions for seasonalisation

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `season_fraction(stock, n_seasons)` | \(\pi_{a,y,s}\); multiply annual gear catch-at-age to get seasonal catch-at-age (observation side) |
| `seasonalize_catch_n_gear(stock, f_age_gear, n_seasons)` | the same seasonal catches computed directly from gear F-at-age |
| `pop_n_season(stock, n_seasons)` | numbers-at-age at the start of each season, \(N_a(0)e^{-Z_a(s-1)/S}\) |
| `survey_n_gear(stock, gear, timing)` | survey numbers-at-age at any time \(t\), \(N_a(0)e^{-Z_at}s_{g,a}\) |
| `lfd.sim.season()` | independent two-stage sample per season, key at \(t_s\) |
| `sel_a_seasonal_avg()`, `wt_a_seasonal()`, `plot_sel_a_seasonal()` | selectivity- and weight-at-age implied by within-year growth, by season and averaged |

### Seasonal catch-at-age

```{r season-fraction}
fr12 <- season_fraction(ple4[, yrs], 12)
range(seasonSums(fr12))                                 # fractions sum to one

cn_m <- cn$Commercial %*% fr12                          # monthly catch-at-age
range(seasonSums(cn_m) / cn$Commercial, na.rm = TRUE)   # = annual catch

# same result from gear F-at-age with seasonalize_catch_n_gear()
F_g <- harvest(ple4)[, yrs]
phi <- F_g; phi[] <- c(gC$f_share)
cn_m2 <- seasonalize_catch_n_gear(ple4[, yrs], list(Commercial = F_g * phi),
                                  n_seasons = 12)$Commercial
range(cn_m2 / cn_m, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r season-fraction-plot, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Fraction of the annual catch taken in each month by age in the last year: ages with high total mortality are caught earlier in the year."}
df_fr <- as.data.frame(fr12[, ac(maxyr)])
df_fr$season <- as.numeric(as.character(df_fr$season))
ggplot(df_fr, aes(season, data, colour = factor(age))) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1 / 12, linetype = 2) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = "Age") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = expression(pi[a*","*s])) + theme_bw()
```

```{r season-catch-plot, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Age composition of the commercial catch by month in the last year: older fish are taken early in the year, before they are fished down."}
df_m <- as.data.frame(cn_m[, ac(maxyr)])
df_m$season <- factor(as.numeric(as.character(df_m$season)))
ggplot(df_m, aes(season, data, fill = factor(age))) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Age") +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Proportion of monthly catch") + theme_bw()
```

## Three sampling designs

The fleet and its length selectivity are the same in all designs; only the
sampling resolution `n_seasons` changes. The total sample sizes are the same
(`ess_age = 200`, `ess_len = 1000` per year), so differences between designs
come from **when** fish are measured, not how many. The IBTS-Q1 survey is
treated as a pulse in mid-January (\(t = 1/24\)) instead of the mid-point of
its Q1 window; its length selectivity is refitted at that timing so that it
keeps the same selectivity-at-age.

```{r designs}
srv_jan  <- 1 / 24
fit_srvJ <- fit_gear_sel(sel_srv, lhpar, ages, "dnormal", timing = srv_jan,
                         grid = grid)

design <- function(n_seasons, ess_age = 200, ess_len = 1000)
  build_design(list(
    Commercial = c(fit_com$cfg, f_mult = 1, ess_age = ess_age,
                   ess_len = ess_len, n_seasons = n_seasons),
    Survey     = c(fit_srvJ$cfg, obs = "survey", ess_age = 250, ess_len = 350,
                   timing = srv_jan)))

designs <- list(Annual = design(1), Quarterly = design(4), Monthly = design(12))

# per-season sample sizes of the commercial gear
lapply(designs, function(d) with(d$Commercial,
  rbind(ess_age = split_ess(ess_age, n_seasons),
        ess_len = split_ess(ess_len, n_seasons))))
```

## Expected annual length composition of the catch

Before sampling, compare the **expected** length composition each design
targets. The year-round catch composition is computed with a fine (weekly)
split; the annual design targets the mid-year snapshot instead.

```{r expected}
sel_vec <- function(g) setNames(c(g$sel_len), dimnames(g$sel_len)$len)
expected_lfd <- function(cn_y, stk_y, gear, S) {
  xs <- cn_y %*% season_fraction(stk_y, S)
  p <- 0
  for (s in seq_len(S)) {
    K <- condition_alk(gear_ialk(gear, timing = (s - 0.5) / S), sel_vec(gear))
    p <- p + c(c(xs[, , , s]) %*% K)
  }
  setNames(p / sum(p), colnames(gear$condALK))
}

yr <- ac(maxyr)
gM <- designs$Monthly$Commercial
p_exp <- lapply(c(Annual = 1, Quarterly = 4, Monthly = 12, `Year-round` = 52),
                function(S) expected_lfd(cn$Commercial[, yr], ple4[, yr], gM, S))
len_mid_g <- an(names(p_exp[[1]])) + grid$bin / 2
round(sapply(p_exp, function(p) c(mean_length = sum(p * len_mid_g),
                                  sd_length = sqrt(sum(p * len_mid_g^2) -
                                                   sum(p * len_mid_g)^2))), 2)
```

```{r expected-plot, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Expected annual length composition of the commercial catch: mid-year snapshot (annual design) against the year-round composition. The year-round composition is broader because each cohort grows during the year."}
df_e <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("Annual", "Year-round"), function(d)
  data.frame(design = d, len = an(names(p_exp[[d]])), p = p_exp[[d]])))
ggplot(df_e, aes(len, p, colour = design)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "Length (cm)", y = "Expected proportion", colour = NULL) + theme_bw()
```

## Simulating the designs: `season = FALSE` and `season = TRUE`

`sample_lfd_gears()` reads the design from each gear. With
`season = FALSE` (default) the seasonal samples are pooled into one annual
sample with `seasonSums()`; with `season = TRUE` they stay in the season
dimension. With the same common random numbers, the two are the same sample:

```{r sim-designs}
sim_y <- ac((maxyr - 4):maxyr)
u_des <- lapply(designs, rUnif_lfd, years = sim_y, nsim = 1, seed = 99)

s_F <- Map(function(d, u) sample_lfd_gears(ple4, d, sim_y, u_lfd = u),
           designs, u_des)
s_T <- sample_lfd_gears(ple4, designs$Monthly, sim_y, u_lfd = u_des$Monthly,
                        season = TRUE)

dim(s_F$Monthly$lfd$Commercial)   # pooled: one season
dim(s_T$lfd$Commercial)           # 12 months
identical(c(seasonSums(s_T$lfd$Commercial)), c(s_F$Monthly$lfd$Commercial))
# fish measured per month (ess_len split among months)
c(seasonSums(quantSums(s_T$lfd$Commercial))[, yr]) ; c(quantSums(s_T$lfd$Commercial)[, yr])
```

```{r ridge-monthly, fig.height = 7, fig.cap = "Monthly commercial length samples (season = TRUE) over the last five years, with von Bertalanffy cohort lines: the cohort modes move up the length axis through the year."}
plot_lfd_ridgeline(list(`Commercial, monthly` = s_T$lfd$Commercial), lhpar = lhpar)
```

With twelve ridges a year the monthly panel is dense. The quarterly design
shows the same within-year progression more clearly: within each year the
cohort modes move up from quarter 1 to quarter 4, and the next year's first
quarter starts again from the lower lengths of the following age.

```{r sim-quarterly}
s_Q <- sample_lfd_gears(ple4, designs$Quarterly, sim_y, u_lfd = u_des$Quarterly,
                        season = TRUE)
dim(s_Q$lfd$Commercial)           # 4 quarters
```

```{r ridge-quarterly, fig.height = 7, fig.cap = "Quarterly commercial length samples (season = TRUE) over the last five years, with von Bertalanffy cohort lines."}
plot_lfd_ridgeline(list(`Commercial, quarterly` = s_Q$lfd$Commercial), lhpar = lhpar)
```

```{r ridge-survey, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "January survey samples: each cohort is measured at the same point of its growth curve, giving sharp modes for the young ages."}
plot_lfd_ridgeline(list(`Survey, January` = s_T$lfd$Survey), lhpar = lhpar)
```

```{r season-lines, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Monthly commercial samples in the last year (season = TRUE)."}
plot_lfd_season(list(Commercial = s_T$lfd$Commercial), year = maxyr)
```

## Contrasting annual and continuous sampling

The pooled annual samples of the three designs, against the year-round
expected composition:

```{r designs-plot, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Annual commercial length samples under the three designs (same total sample size) and the expected year-round composition (dashed)."}
plot_lfd_designs(lapply(s_F, function(s) s$lfd$Commercial), year = maxyr,
                 expected = p_exp$`Year-round`)
```

The replicated effective sample size makes the contrast quantitative. Each
design is evaluated against two targets: its **own** expectation (precision)
and the **year-round** composition (what the fishery actually caught). A
sample that is precise for the wrong target has a high ESS against its own
expectation but a lower one against the year-round composition, because the
systematic difference does not shrink with sample size.

```{r ess-designs}
nrep    <- 200
stk_rep <- propagate(ple4[, yr], nrep)
ess_tab <- sapply(names(designs), function(d) {
  S <- designs[[d]]$Commercial$n_seasons
  x <- sample_lfd_gears(stk_rep, designs[[d]], yr)$lfd$Commercial
  c(own_expectation = median(ess_mi(x, p_exp[[d]])),
    year_round      = median(ess_mi(x, p_exp$`Year-round`)))
})
round(ess_tab)
```

Reading the table:

* All designs measure the same number of fish, and the age (cluster) stage
  limits the effective sample size well below `ess_len` in every design.
* The **annual** design is evaluated against the mid-year snapshot. Against
  the year-round composition its ESS drops, by how much depends on how much
  the stock grows within the year relative to the length-at-age spread.
* The **monthly** design targets (almost) the year-round composition by
  construction; quarterly lies in between.
* For an assessment that treats the year as one time step, the pooled monthly
  sample (`season = FALSE`) is the appropriate input. For a seasonal
  assessment, `season = TRUE` passes each month with its own timing, and the
  January survey adds a sharp snapshot at the start of the growing season.

# Part III: length sampling inside an MSE with `sampling.lfd.oem()`

`sampling.lfd.oem()` is an `FLoem` method with the same structure as
`mse::sampling.oem()`. For each data year it calls `sample_lfd_gears()` on
the OM stock (by unit) and reports catch weight by fishery gear. The samples
reach the estimator as attributes of the observed stock, `attr(stk, "lfd")`
and `attr(stk, "catch_gear")`, because `mp()` passes only `stk` and `idx` to
the `est` module. The design (annual, quarterly, monthly; survey timing) comes
from the gears, and `season` decides whether seasonal samples are pooled.

## Operating model

```{r om, eval = run_mse}
nsim <- 20
iy   <- maxyr
fy   <- iy + 15
y0   <- iy - 9                               # first year of the LFD series

sr  <- FLSRTMB::srrTMB(as.FLSR(ple4, model = bevholtSV), spr0 = mean(spr0y(ple4)))
brp <- computeFbrp(ple4, sr, proxy = "msy", blim = 0.25, type = "btgt", verbose = FALSE)
fmsy <- c(refpts(brp)["msy", "harvest"])
bmsy <- c(refpts(brp)["msy", "ssb"])

om <- FLom(stock = propagate(ple4, nsim), sr = sr, refpts = refpts(brp),
           projection = mseCtrl(method = fwd.om),
           deviances = rlnormar1(n = nsim, sdlog = 0.4, rho = 0.3, years = iy:fy))
om <- fwdWindow(om, end = fy)
```

## Observation error model

`lfd_obs_init()` builds `observations$lfd` and `observations$catch_gear` from
`y0` to `fy` and fills the historical years with `sample_lfd_gears()`, using
the same common random numbers as the OEM. `deviances$lfd` holds the common
random numbers for every year, so each deviate is used once.

```{r oem-fun, eval = run_mse}
make_oem <- function(gears, season = FALSE, seed = 123) {
  u_lfd <- rUnif_lfd(gears, years = y0:fy, nsim = nsim, seed = seed)
  init  <- lfd_obs_init(stock(om), gears, years = y0:fy, hist_years = y0:iy,
                        u_lfd = u_lfd, season = season)
  cg_dev <- FLQuants(lapply(init$catch_gear, function(x)    # ~10% CV
    rlnorm(nsim, FLQuant(0, dimnames = list(year = y0:fy)), 0.1)))
  FLoem(method = sampling.lfd.oem,
        observations = list(stk = stock(om), lfd = init$lfd,
                            catch_gear = init$catch_gear),
        deviances    = list(lfd = u_lfd, catch_gear = cg_dev),
        args         = list(om_gears = gears, season = season))
}
oem_a <- make_oem(designs$Annual)                    # annual design
oem_q <- make_oem(designs$Quarterly, season = TRUE)  # quarterly, kept by quarter
```

## Management procedure

The estimator here is a placeholder that checks the LFD channel and then acts
as a perfect assessment; in the FLicc MSE it is replaced by `flicc.sa()`.

```{r ctrl, eval = run_mse}
lfd.check.sa <- function(stk, idx, args, tracking, ...) {
  lfd <- attr(stk, "lfd")
  dy  <- args$dy
  track(tracking, "lfd.n.Commercial", ac(args$ay)) <-
    quantSums(seasonSums(window(lfd$Commercial, start = dy, end = dy)))
  perfect.sa(stk, idx, args, tracking)
}

ctrl <- mpCtrl(list(
  est  = mseCtrl(method = lfd.check.sa),
  hcr  = mseCtrl(method = hockeystick.hcr,
                 args = list(lim = 0, trigger = 0.5 * bmsy, target = fmsy,
                             min = 0, metric = "ssb", output = "fbar")),
  isys = mseCtrl(method = tac.is, args = list(recyrs = -2, fmin = 0))))

mseargs <- list(iy = iy, fy = fy, y0 = y0, data_lag = 1, management_lag = 1,
                frq = 1, it = nsim)
```

`parallel = FALSE` is required for now: when `mp()` splits iterations across
workers it subsets only `FLQuant` deviances, while the common random numbers
from `rUnif_lfd()` are plain arrays (see the developer notes).

```{r run, eval = run_mse}
# the cache stores the settings it was built with; any change in the
# sampling design, nsim or years triggers a re-run instead of a stale load
run_or_load <- function(file, oem, gears) {
  sig <- list(design = lapply(gears, `[`, c("obs", "ess_age", "ess_len", "n_seasons")),
              timing = sapply(gears, function(g) g$grid$timing),
              season = args(oem)$season, nsim = nsim, years = c(y0, iy, fy))
  if (file.exists(file)) {
    cached <- readRDS(file)
    if (is.list(cached) && identical(cached$sig, sig)) return(cached$run)
    message("Cached MSE in ", basename(file), " was built with other settings: re-running.")
  }
  run <- mp(om, oem = oem, ctrl = ctrl, args = mseargs, parallel = FALSE,
            verbose = FALSE)
  dir.create(dirname(file), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  saveRDS(list(run = run, sig = sig), file)
  run
}
run_a <- run_or_load(f_mse_a, oem_a, designs$Annual)
run_q <- run_or_load(f_mse_q, oem_q, designs$Quarterly)
```

## Checks on the MSE output

```{r mse-checks, eval = run_mse}
check_run <- function(run, oem0, gears) {
  lfd_run <- observations(oem(run))$lfd
  lfd_ini <- observations(oem0)$lfd
  cg_run  <- observations(oem(run))$catch_gear
  hy <- ac(y0:iy)

  # years sampled by the OEM: mp() samples dy = ay - data_lag for each
  # management year ay (iy - 1 up to fy - 3 with these settings)
  yrs_run <- dimnames(lfd_run$Commercial)$year
  n_mat   <- matrix(c(quantSums(seasonSums(lfd_run$Commercial))),
                    nrow = length(yrs_run))
  proj    <- setdiff(yrs_run[rowSums(n_mat > 0) == nsim], hy)

  by_gear <- t(sapply(names(gears), function(g) c(
    ess_len = gears[[g]]$ess_len,
    # fish per sampled projection year and iteration (should equal ess_len)
    fish_min = min(quantSums(seasonSums(lfd_run[[g]][, proj]))),
    fish_max = max(quantSums(seasonSums(lfd_run[[g]][, proj]))),
    # common random numbers: the OEM re-samples the last historical year
    # with the same deviates and catch, so the seed is reproduced
    history_reproduced = identical(c(lfd_run[[g]][, hy]), c(lfd_ini[[g]][, hy])))))
  list(projection_years = range(an(proj)),
       by_gear = by_gear,
       seasons = sapply(lfd_run, function(x) dim(x)[4]),
       # (3) reported/true catch: the reporting error (~10% CV)
       catch_ratio = summary(c(cg_run$Commercial[, proj] /
                               catch(run@om@stock)[, proj])))
}
check_run(run_a, oem_a, designs$Annual)
check_run(run_q, oem_q, designs$Quarterly)
```

```{r mse-plot, eval = run_mse, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "Historical OM and MP projections with the annual and the quarterly sampling design (the placeholder estimator is a perfect assessment, so the two MPs differ only through implementation)."}
rp_plot <- FLPar(Fmsy = fmsy, Bmsy = bmsy, Btrigger = 0.5 * bmsy)
plotAdvice(FLStocks(OM = window(stock(om), end = iy),
                    Annual = window(run_a@om@stock, start = iy),
                    Quarterly = window(run_q@om@stock, start = iy)),
           rpts = rp_plot)
```

```{r mse-lfd-plot, eval = run_mse, fig.height = 7, fig.cap = "Quarterly commercial samples for iteration 1 as passed to est with season = TRUE: the last historical years and the first projection years."}
lfd_q <- observations(oem(run_q))$lfd$Commercial
yrs_q <- dimnames(lfd_q)$year[c(quantSums(seasonSums(iter(lfd_q, 1)))) > 0]
yrs_q <- head(yrs_q[an(yrs_q) >= iy - 3], 8)
# time runs along the (flipped) y aesthetic: dashed line = start of projection
plot_lfd_ridgeline(list(`Commercial, quarterly` = iter(lfd_q[, yrs_q], 1)), lhpar = lhpar) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = iy + 1, linetype = 2)
```

```{r mse-lfd-season, eval = run_mse, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Quarterly commercial samples in the first sampled projection year (iteration 1), one line per quarter."}
plot_lfd_season(list(Commercial = iter(lfd_q, 1)), year = yrs_q[an(yrs_q) > iy][1])
```

# Towards sex-structured and spatial stocks

The single-sex machinery extends to stocks with a populated `unit` dimension,
but `unit` means two different things, and the sampling design differs:

| | `unit.type = "gender"` (Doc 2) | `unit.type = "spatial"` (Doc 3) |
|---|---|---|
| units | `"F"`, `"M"` | areas |
| growth | sex-specific `lhpar[, u]` | usually shared |
| gear selectivity-at-length | shared \(s_g(l)\); \(s_{g,a,u}\) differs through growth | area-specific gear sets possible |
| sampling event | **one** sample per gear from the combined catch; sexes are labels on fish | **independent** samples per area |
| ESS | `ess_age`, `ess_len` shared across sexes | per area |
| CRN streams | one per gear | one per area and gear |
| pooling for `est` | sum over units (no raising needed: sampling is proportional to catch) | raise to catch by area (`lfd.raising = TRUE`) and pool |
| length grid | must be common across sexes | common |
| within-year design | as Part II, per gear (`n_seasons`, survey `timing`) | as Part II, per area and gear |

Two choices follow for `sampling.lfd.oem()`:

* a new argument `unit.type = c("gender", "spatial")`, with the current
  behaviour as `"spatial"`; and
* for `"gender"`, the joint draw over (sex, age) and then (sex, length) can
  reuse `lfd.sim()` unchanged by stacking the sexes into one block-diagonal
  conditional key, season by season with `season_fraction()` computed per sex.

For the life-history parameters, an `FLPar` with a `unit` dimension
(`params x unit x iter`) is preferable to `FLPars`: subsetting `lhpar[, "F"]`
mirrors `stk[, , "F"]`, iterations propagate in one object, and a single
argument passes through `build_gear()`. The developer notes give the details.

# Appendix A: length-based utilities in FLRef

All functions are exported unless marked *internal*. Arguments in *italics*
default to the gear's settings (`gear$grid`, `gear$lhpar`).

## A.1 Growth, length grid and keys

| Function | Purpose | Key arguments | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `iALK()` | inverse age-length key \(P(l\mid a,t)\), normal length-at-age around a growth curve | `params`, `model`, `age`, `cv`, `lmin`, `lmax`, `bin`, `max`, `reflen` | `FLPar` age x len |
| `len_grid()` | the single length grid (lower bin limits; last bin a plus group) | `linf`, `lmin`, `lmax_mult`, `bin` | numeric |
| `gear_ialk()` | \(P(l\mid a,t)\) on a gear's own grid, at any `timing` | `gear`, `age`, `timing`, `params` | matrix age x len |
| `condition_alk()` | capture-conditioned key \(P(l\mid a,g)\) from \(P(l\mid a)\) and \(s_g(l)\) | `ialk_mat`, `sel_len_vec` | matrix age x len |
| `ALK()` | age-length key \(P(a\mid l)\) for one sampling event | `N_a`, `iALK` | `FLPar` |
| `ALKs()` | annual keys \(P(a\mid l)\) from at-age numbers and a (conditioned) inverse key | `object`, `iALK` | `FLPars` by year |

## A.2 Selectivity and gears

| Function | Purpose | Key arguments | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sel_logistic_len()`, `sel_normal_len()`, `sel_dnormal_len()` | selectivity-at-length shapes | `L`, shape parameters | numeric |
| `sel_la()` | stand-alone selectivity-at-length and ALK-integrated selectivity-at-age | `lhpar`, `type`, shape parameters | list |
| `combine_sel_age()` | joint selectivity-at-age weighted by relative apical F | `object`, `fapic_rel` | `FLQuant` |
| `build_gear()` | gear objects: \(s_g(l)\), \(s_{g,a}\), \(P(l\mid a,g)\), F shares, weight-at-length and sampling design (`obs`, `timing`, `n_seasons`, `ess_age`, `ess_len`) | `gear_cfg`, `lhpar`, `age`, `timing`, `fbar_range`, grid | list of gears |
| `gear_par()` | one scalar entry across gears | `om_gears`, `what` | named vector |
| `joint_sel()` | selectivity of total F implied by the gears (Fbar scale) | `om_gears` | `FLQuant` |
| `f_age_gear()` | gear F-at-age from gear Fbar trajectories | `stock`, `om_gears`, `fbar_gear` | `FLQuants` |
| `f_share_gear()` | time-varying share of total F-at-age by gear | `f_age` | `FLQuants` |
| `sel_a_seasonal_avg()` | selectivity-at-age averaged over within-year growth | `lhpar`, `sel_len`, `age`, `n_seasons` | numeric |
| `wt_a_seasonal()` | weight-at-age averaged over seasons, weighted by seasonal numbers | `n_season`, `params`, *`gear`*, `n_seasons` | `FLQuant` |

## A.3 Catch partition and within-year allocation

| Function | Purpose | Key arguments | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `catch_n_gear()` | partial Baranov catch-at-age by gear (sums to the total) | `stock`, `shares`, `years` | `FLQuants` (+ `attr(, "total")`) |
| `catch_gear()` | annual catch (weight or numbers) by gear | `catch_n`, `wt`, `type` | `FLQuants` |
| `catch_by_gear()` | relative catch by gear over a window (FLicc input) | `catch_n`, `wt`, `years`, `iter` | vector / matrix |
| `season_fraction()` | share \(\pi_{a,y,s}\) of the annual catch taken in each season | `stock`, `n_seasons` | `FLQuant` with seasons |
| `seasonalize_catch_n_gear()` | seasonal gear catch-at-age from gear F-at-age | `stock`, `f_age_gear`, `n_seasons` | `FLQuants` |
| `pop_n_season()` | numbers-at-age at the start of each season | `stock`, `n_seasons` | `FLQuant` |
| `survey_n_gear()` | survey numbers-at-age at the survey timing | `stock`, `gear`, `years`, *`timing`* | `FLQuant` |

## A.4 Sampling

| Function | Purpose | Key arguments | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ca.sim()` | multinomial catch-at-age sample (stage 1) | `object`, `ess`, `u` | `FLQuant` |
| `len.sim()` | single-stage length sample, optional gear key, several timings | `N_a`, `params`, `ess`, `timing`, `gear`, `u` | `FLQuant` |
| `lfd.sim()` | two-stage length sample (age, then length) | `object`, `gear`, *`ess_age`*, *`ess_len`*, `timing`, `u_age`, `u_len`, `scale` | `FLQuant` |
| `lfd.sim.season()` | independent two-stage sample per season, key at mid-season | `object` (seasonal), `gear`, `n_seasons`, `u_age`, `u_len`, `season` | `FLQuant` |
| `sample_lfd_gears()` | all gears of one unit: fishery (annual or within-year) and surveys; the OEM's sampling step | `stock`, `om_gears`, `years`, `u_lfd`, `f_share`, `season` | list(`lfd`, `catch_n`) |
| `split_ess()` | exact split of a sample size among seasons | `n`, `S` | integer |
| `rmultinom_crn()` | multinomial draw from pre-generated uniforms (common random numbers) | `u`, `p` | integer counts |
| `rUnif_len()`, `rUnif_lfd()` | common random numbers for `len.sim()` / `lfd.sim()` (seasonal streams for `n_seasons > 1`) | `gear(s)`, `years`, `nsim`, `seed` | list of arrays |
| `idx.sim()` | age-based survey index with observation error | `object`, `sel`, `ess`, `sigma`, `q` | `FLIndex` |

## A.5 From lengths to ages and raising

| Function | Purpose | Key arguments | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `alk.sample()` | length-stratified otolith subsample of annual ALKs (at most `nbin` per length class) | `lfds`, `alks`, `nbin`, `n.sample` | `FLPars` (counts) |
| `applyALK()` | numbers-at-age from a length sample and annual ALKs | `lfds`, `alks` | `FLQuant` |
| `lfd_sop()` | raise a length sample to catch weight by sum of products with \(W(l)\) (seasonal samples: one factor per year) | `lfd`, `wt_len`, `catch` | `FLQuant` |
| `sops()` | raise catch-at-age to the stock's catch weight (optional error) | `object`, `stock`, `sigma` | `FLQuant` |
| `pgquant()` | set a plus group on an at-age `FLQuant` | `object`, `pg` | `FLQuant` |

## A.6 MSE observation model

| Function | Purpose | Key arguments | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sampling.lfd.oem()` | `FLoem` method: length samples and reported catch by gear for each data year | `om_gears`, `f_share`, `season`, `lfd.raising`, `lfd.scale` | list(`stk`, `idx`, `observations`, `tracking`) |
| `lfd_obs_init()` | builds `observations$lfd` / `$catch_gear` and seeds the historical years with the OEM's own code and random numbers | `stock`, `om_gears`, `years`, `hist_years`, `u_lfd`, `season` | list |
| `lfd_template()` | empty length-sample `FLQuant` for a gear, with the right season dimension | `gear`, `years`, `nsim`, `units`, `season` | `FLQuant` |
| `.lfd_gears_by_unit()`, `.lfd_crn_by_unit()`, `.lfd_flat_gears()` | *internal*: normalise gear and random-number lists by unit | | |

## A.7 Plots

| Function | Shows |
|---|---|
| `plot_sel_la()` | selectivity-at-length and -at-age side by side |
| `plot_sel_age()` | one or more selectivity-at-age curves |
| `plot_condALK()` | \(P(l\mid a,g)\) heat map, optionally with biological vs. conditioned mean length-at-age |
| `plot_condALK_bias()` | mean length-at-age in the population and in the catch, all gears |
| `plot_sel_a_seasonal()` | selectivity-at-age by season implied by within-year growth |
| `plot_lfd_ridgeline()` | length samples as ridgelines along time (annual or seasonal), with cohort growth lines |
| `plot_lfd_season()` | seasonal length samples for one year, by gear |
| `plot_lfd_designs()` | pooled annual composition of several sampling designs, with an expected composition |

# Appendix B: notation

| Symbol | Meaning | In code |
|---|---|---|
| \(a, l, y, s, g\) | age, length class (lower limit), year, season, gear | dimnames `age`, `len`, `year`, `season`; gear names |
| \(N_{a,y}\), \(F_{a,y}\), \(M_{a,y}\), \(Z_{a,y}\) | numbers at 1 January, fishing, natural and total mortality | `stock.n`, `harvest`, `m` |
| \(\phi_{g,a}\) | share of total F-at-age taken by gear \(g\) | `gear$f_share`, `f_share_gear()` |
| \(C_{g,a,y}\), \(C_{g,a,y,s}\) | gear catch-at-age, annual and by season | `catch_n_gear()`, `season_fraction()` |
| \(\pi_{a,y,s}\) | share of the annual catch taken in season \(s\) | `season_fraction()` |
| \(P(l\mid a,t)\) | biological inverse key at within-year time \(t\) | `iALK()`, `gear_ialk()` |
| \(s_g(l)\), \(s_{g,a}\) | selectivity-at-length, ALK-integrated selectivity-at-age | `gear$sel_len`, `gear$sel_a` |
| \(K_{a,l}=P(l\mid a,g)\) | capture-conditioned key | `gear$condALK`, `condition_alk()` |
| \(P(a\mid l,g)\) | age-length key of the catch | `ALKs()` with `gear$condALK` |
| \(n_A\), \(n_L\) | stage-1 (age) and stage-2 (length) sample sizes | `ess_age`, `ess_len` |
| \(W(l)=a\bar l^{\,b}\) | weight at length (bin mid-point) | `gear$wt_len` |
